en: Influence is {col:stakeholders.influence} and interest is {col:stakeholders.interest}, so the engagement is: {col:stakeholders.quadrant}. Their attitude is {col:stakeholders.attitude} and the action is: {col:stakeholders.action}.
The project manager reviews this entry at every gate and after every steering meeting.
The RACI matrix lists {col:projects.raci_n} activities. Of these, {col:projects.raci_bad} need a fix: each activity needs one person who is responsible and exactly one person who is accountable.
Everyone named in the matrix confirms their role before the kick-off. Anyone consulted is asked before a decision, and anyone informed is told after it.
We ask for {col:funding.requested} and ask you to approve it under the budget code {col:funding.budget_code}. The request was made on {col:funding.requested_on}.
Current state: {col:funding.state}. Amount approved so far: {col:funding.approved}. Amount not approved: {col:funding.short}.
Please approve the amount, or tell us what you need to change, so that the finance partner can open the budget.
Portfolio overview line for the leadership team
Project: {col:projects.name} for {col:projects.client}. Type: {col:projects.type}. Method: {col:projects.method}. Priority: {col:projects.priority}. Stage: {col:projects.stage}.
Status: {col:projects.status}. Health: {col:projects.health}. Progress: {col:projects.pct_done}. The budget is {col:projects.budget}, which is {col:projects.share} of the portfolio budget.
The baseline end is {col:projects.end} and the forecast end is {col:projects.forecast_end}. Days late: {col:projects.days_late}. Schedule: {col:projects.schedule}.
The leadership team is asked to note the position and to decide on any project that shows red health or a late end date.
You are invited to the kick-off of the project, which starts on {col:projects.start}. The project runs until {col:projects.end}.

Agenda: 1. Purpose and objectives from the charter. 2. Scope, what is in and what is out. 3. Roles, using the RACI matrix. 4. Plan, milestones and the budget of {col:projects.budget}. 5. Risks and assumptions. 6. How we report and decide. 7. Next steps.
Please confirm that you will attend and send us anything you want on the agenda.
Project start-up confirmation to the client
We confirm that the project {col:projects.name} is approved. Your sponsor is {col:projects.sponsor} and our project manager is {col:projects.manager}.
The start date is {col:projects.start} and the planned end date is {col:projects.end}. The budget is {col:projects.budget}.
In the first two weeks we will hold a scope workshop and agree the charter and the plan with you. Please name the people from your side who will take part.

Open Start and type your company name and your own limits in the yellow cells: the score a proposal needs, the days a proposal may wait, the payback you accept and your warning days.
Fill Portfolio Register with every project: client, sponsor, manager, dates, budget, status, stage, priority, health and progress. Days late and the schedule state fill in.
List new ideas on Project Proposals. Set the criteria and weights on Scoring Criteria, then score every proposal on Priority Scoring; rank and the cut-off check fill in.
Write a business case for each proposal on Business Cases. Net present value, payback and a verdict fill in, and missing figures are flagged.
Keep one charter per project on Project Charters and record the date it was signed. A charter that waits too long turns overdue to sign.
Agree what is in and out on Scope Register, the success measures on Success Measures, and the assumptions on Assumptions.
Rate every stakeholder on Stakeholder Register and fill RACI Matrix with one accountable person for each activity.
Run the six gate checks on Stage Gates, and write each go, defer or no-go on Go No-go Decisions with its conditions and review date.
Record funding requests on Funding Approvals, staffing needs on Staffing Requests, and the planned and actual spend of each quarter on Quarterly Budget.
Rate each project against the six objectives on Strategy Alignment and write the monthly decision for each project on Portfolio Review Log.
Use the 14 calculators for business case value, priority score, project price, contingency, estimates, team size, scope change, readiness, cost of delay, break-even, capacity, funding and win rate.
Print 10 sheets and 10 letters, follow 10 checklists and tap a message link to open a message with the text ready.
Read Portfolio Dashboard and Charts every week and before each portfolio review.
Plan, schedule and keep every project on its dates
Plan tasks, dates, baselines and delays for every project
Task list with live state and days late
every task shows done, blocked, overdue, start late, slipping or due soon from your dates and percent done, with the owner and manager phones beside it
Dependency check with link types and lags
finish to start, start to start and finish to finish links with a lag or a lead are checked against the dates, and missing or circular links are flagged
Milestones with baseline and forecast dates
slip in days, days left and a met-on-time check for every milestone, with the sponsor and client contact one tap away
every version of a project baseline, who approved it, why it was reset and how far the end date moved from the version before
baseline and forecast end, percent done and slip for each phase of each project, worked out from the tasks of that phase
Working-day calendar with holidays and leave
every end date skips weekends and your company holidays, and leave that meets a task or a release is flagged
Three-point estimates with a width check
best, likely and worst hours give expected hours, the range and a width warning; finished tasks show actual against estimated hours by phase
twelve weeks of tasks starting and due, hours at an even pace, people away and holidays against capacity, with heavy and light weeks marked
tasks with little float get a driver, a watch owner and an action with a date, marked critical, watch or under control from your float limit
Delay register with cause and recovery action
each late task has a cause, an owner and a recovery date, and the register shows which recoveries are overdue and what causes most delay
Release dates with freeze and window checks
the code freeze date, working days left and a check of closure days and leave for each release
Fixed dates with spare days and penalty exposure
contract and client dates are compared with your forecast to show spare days and the penalty you would pay for the weeks late
Days ahead that count as due soon

Estimate range that makes an estimate wide
Share of a day that is real project work
Spare days that count as tight
Weekly load above which a week is heavy
Weekly load below which a week is light
Projects: baseline, forecast and schedule health
One row for each project with its baseline end and today forecast end; slip, schedule colour, progress from the task list, next milestone and a phase-by-phase summary fill in by themselves.
Extra hours a week to hold baseline
Phone number of the project manager
Phone number of the PMO lead
Team: who can take the work and who is away
One row for each team member with role, cost per hour and weekly hours; open tasks, hours still to do, weeks of work queued and leave status fill in by themselves.
Work breakdown: phases and work packages with hours
One row for each phase and work package with its code, owner and top-down hours; the tasks linked to it, their hours and a check against your estimate fill in.
Task list: dates, owner, progress and what the schedule says
One row for each task with owner, baseline dates, hours, progress and your forecast end; working days, days late, the state and the owner and manager phones fill in by themselves.
Phone number of the task owner
Task dependencies: links, lags and a check for broken links
One row for each link between a task and its predecessor, with link type and lag in days (a negative lag is a lead); both task dates and a check for missing, circular or conflicting links fill in.
Name of the task that has the link
Milestones: baseline, forecast and actual dates
One row for each milestone with its baseline, forecast and actual date; slip in days, days left, a date check and the sponsor and client contact phones fill in.
Phone number of the client contact
Schedule baselines: every approved plan and how it moved
One row for each version of a project baseline with its dates and the reason; duration, the end of the version before, how far the end moved and the approver phone fill in.
Phase plan: seven phases for every project
One row for each project and phase with its baseline dates; forecast end, progress, slip and a state are worked out from the tasks of that phase.
Schedule changes: what moved, why and who approved it
One row for each change of a task end date with the old and new date, the reason and the approver; the shift in days and working days and the phones of the task owner and the client contact fill in.
Name of the task that moved
Owner of the task that moved
Delay register: late tasks, cause and recovery action
One row for each late task with its cause, recovery action, owner and due date; days late come from the task list and a state shows which recoveries are overdue.
Project that holds the late task
Company holidays: closure days that the plan must skip
One row for each company closure day; the weekday, days to go and a state fill in, and every date here is skipped by the working-day counts in the whole workbook.
Leave calendar: who is away and what it does to the plan
One row for each leave with person, type, dates and approver; working days, open tasks and releases that fall inside the leave and a clash check fill in.
Role of the person on leave
Phone number of the person on leave
Working days by month: holidays and team hours
One row for each month (the first day of the month); calendar days, weekend days, holidays, working days, team hours and leave fill in from the holiday and leave sheets.
Three-point estimates: expected hours and range
One row for each estimated task with optimistic, likely and pessimistic hours; expected hours, the range, a width check and a comparison with the task estimate fill in.
Releases and go-live dates: freeze, window and contact
One row for each release or go-live with its date, scope and owner; the freeze date, working days left and a window check against closure days and leave fill in.
Phone number of the release owner
External dependencies: what you wait for
One row for each item the plan waits for from a client or a vendor, with the contact, our owner and the date it is needed; days waiting and a state fill in by themselves.
Fixed dates: spare days and penalty exposure
One row for each date that cannot move, with its source and the penalty per week; spare days against the forecast, a state and the penalty exposure fill in.
Weekly look-ahead: twelve weeks of tasks and load
One row for each week (type the Monday); tasks starting and due, hours at an even pace, late tasks, people away, capacity and the load fill in, with the next three weeks shown beside the first.
Critical items: tasks with little float and who watches
One row for each task you watch every Monday with its float in days, the driver, the watch owner and the action; the state against your float limit and the task details fill in.
Name of the task you watch
Phone number of the watch owner
Estimate accuracy: estimated against actual hours
One row for each finished task with the hours it really took; the estimate, the factor, a check against your limit and the average factor of the phase fill in.
